sections.label: Parliamentary questions on energy imports
sections.summary: Questions ask the Minister for Trade and Industry about domestic generation options, import caps, Sun Cable, diversification, fuel mix and renewable targets.

sentences.speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what domestic energy generation options the Ministry had considered prior to proposing the import of electricity from regional countries; (b) whether the Ministry plans to (i) set a cap on the proportion of imported energy as part of our overall energy supply and (ii) set a cap on the amount that individual countries can export energy to Singapore, in order to limit the risk to Singapore's energy security; and (c) what other steps the Ministry will be taking to ensure Singapore's energy security when the trial is expanded.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) whether Singapore will be participating in the Sun Cable project; (b) if so, how much of Singapore's energy supply will come from the Sun Cable project; (c) what efforts are in place to diversify our energy sources; and (d) what are the associated risks and cost fluctuations of energy diversification.

sentences.speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) how have post-COVID-19 needs impacted Singapore's energy market outlook; (b) whether Singapore's plan to import electricity from Malaysia is limited to renewable energy; (c) what is the process for the energy to be sold to Singapore; and (d) how can energy supply reliability be assured as more clean electricity from other countries are imported into Singapore.

sentences.speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
sentences.text: asked the Minister for Trade and Industry (a) what is the current fuel mix for electricity generation derived from renewable energy sources; (b) how has this changed over the last 10 years; and (c) what is the target mix for the amount of electricity generated from renewable energy sources in 2030 and 2050.

sections.label: Natural gas share of electricity
sections.summary: Natural gas accounts for 95% of Singapore's electricity production and Singapore lacks alternative energy sources.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: Natural gas currently accounts for 95% of the electricity produced in Singapore and I think all Members here in this House would appreciate the fact that we lack alternative energy sources.

sections.label: Solar capacity growth targets
sections.summary: Installed solar capacity rose from 3.8 megawatt-peak in 2010 to about 400 megawatt-peak in mid-2020, with targets of 1.5 gigawatt-peak by 2025 and 2 gigawatt-peak by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: Over the last 10 years, installed solar capacity has increased more than a hundred fold, from 3.8 megawatt-peak in 2010, to around 400 megawatt-peak last year, in mid-2020.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: We are accelerating our efforts and will almost quadruple our solar capacity to 1.5 gigawatt-peak by 2025 – five years from now – and, by the end of 2030, we hope to achieve 2 gigawatt-peak.

sections.label: Trial electricity imports from Malaysia
sections.summary: Singapore is trialling imports of up to 100 megawatts from Peninsular Malaysia.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: For a start, we are trialling imports of up to 100 megawatts from Peninsular Malaysia.

sections.label: Low-Carbon Energy Research Funding Initiative
sections.summary: A Low-Carbon Energy Research Funding Initiative will use around $50 million to explore hydrogen supply, storage and downstream uses, and carbon capture and storage.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: We will facilitate the development of these technologies through various research, development and demonstration funding initiatives, including a Low-Carbon Energy Research Funding Initiative.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: This initiative will see around $50 million being used to explore areas such as the supply, storage and downstream uses of hydrogen, as well as carbon capture and storage for use in building materials or fuels.

sections.label: Emissions peak and 2050 target
sections.summary: The breakdown is 95% natural gas, with carbon emissions expected to peak at about 65 million tonnes by 2030 and halve by 2050.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: With regard to the percentage breakdown of the four switches, at this particular point in time, it is 95% natural gas.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: The natural fossil fuels which we, as I have alluded to earlier is the cleanest fossil fuel today.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: It is difficult to give a percentage breakdown but suffice to say that by 2030, we expect to peak in terms of carbon emission at about 65 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emission.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: Our target is to halve that by 2050.

sections.label: Solar power renewable energy targets
sections.summary: The two gigawatt peak of renewable solar power will come in by 2030, with 1.5 gigawatt on track by 2025.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: With regard to the renewable energy targets, the two gigawatt peak in terms of solar power, the renewable solar power, will come in by 2030.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: We are on track by 2025 to achieve 1.5 gigawatt.

sections.label: Regional power grid import pricing
sections.summary: The pricing from importing 100 megawatt from the regional power grid should not be significantly higher than today's electricity tariffs.

sentences.speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
sentences.text: When we work out the arithmetic behind it, from the import of the 100 megawatt from the regional power grid, the pricing should not be significantly higher than what we are already getting today in terms of the electricity tariffs.
